newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine stocks pull back, seen firm.
newsitem.headline: Argentine stocks pull back, seen firm.

text.p: Argentine stocks staged a sharp retreat Thursday on slack volume but were seen keeping a firm underlying tone, dealers said.
"Bidding dried up after two days of action and the market surrendered part of its recent gains, but it may test resistance levels again Friday," said Jose Napoli of brokers Ignoto y Napoli.

The blue-chip MerVal index slumped 1.7 percent to 709.78. It had risen 3.4 percent in the previous two sessions, cheered by Standard & Poor's decision to grant investment-grade credit ratings to several local companies.
"The MerVal pulled back just before 723 today but it may head for 725 in the next two or three sessions, always staying highly selective" Napoli said.
Floor volume slowed to 21 million pesos from 29.6 million Wednesday while over-the-counter deals shrank to 110.9 million pesos from Wednesday's hefty tally of 185.5 million pesos.

"If we'd got a little help from New York today things might have been different. But the markets were weak there, causing cash flows to fizzle, and locally export sector stocks were hurt by the trade row with Brazil," an analyst at a foreign investment bank said.

Brazil last month imposed caps on import financing which could hurt Argentine exports. But analysts said a weekend meeting in Rio by Presidents Carlos Menem of Argentina and Fernando Cardoso of Brazil could help resolve the issue.
The broad market eased 0.3 percent Thursday, with losers outstripping winners 31 to 13 and 20 stocks closing flat.
Heaviest main-tier losses were run up by steelmaker Acindar, carmaker Sevel and footwear and textile firm Alpargatas, which tumbled 4.8 percent, 4.0 percent and 3.0 percent, respectively.

The only MerVal gainers were pulp and paper maker Celulosa, which continued its rollercoaster ride with a 3.6 percent jump after recent heavy losses, real estate developer Irsa, which tacke on 1.4 percent, and Telecom and Telefonica, up 1.9 percent and 1.0 percent, respectively.
